paras: The lynching of Irvin Love was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Norfield, Lincoln County, Mississippi, on the night of Wednesday, August 22, 1900. Love, accused of robbing and burning a house and said to have confessed, was taken from custody while awaiting the sheriff and found hanged from a gum tree the next morning. A New Orleans wire story carried the killing to papers in New York and Washington, while the Brookhaven Leader described how the sheriff had been decoyed away.

According to the Brookhaven Leader, the house of Joe Sasser burned while Sasser and his family were attending church at Gum Grove. Suspicion fell on Love, described as about 20 or 21, after he was seen in Bogue Chitto offering to trade a pistol later identified as Sasser's. He was found working for the Enochs Lumber Company at Fernwood, where R. L. Brent of Bogue Chitto arrested him and brought him back.

Arraigned before Justice R. R. Albritton of Beat 4 on charges of burglary, theft and arson, Love was said to have pleaded guilty and confessed that he set the fire to hide the theft of a revolver, a razor and a bottle of whisky. The wire account added that he returned most of the stolen property.

As news of the confession spread, the Leader reported "suppressed excitement and indignation" in the neighborhood, and Albritton, fearing violence, locked Love in a back room of his residence rather than send him to Brookhaven with the acting constable. Sheriff Applewhite received a telephone message that Wednesday afternoon and took a train to Norfield. At the depot a young man told him the prisoner had already been taken by a mob, and on the road a stranger posing as Albritton's messenger sent him to a spot on the Bogue Chitto road where the mob would supposedly hang Love.

The sheriff waited there with the false messenger and two other men, but no mob came, and he concluded he was being played by "friends of the lynchers." The mob, the Leader reported, took Love only around the time the sheriff got back to Norfield, its friends having learned of his coming because Albritton had made it public. The next morning Love was found hanging from a gum tree by a grass rope on the Summit road, a few hundred yards south of Mt. Pleasant Church.

Circuit Clerk Oliver, acting as coroner, empaneled a jury, which returned a verdict that Love had died at the hands of parties unknown. Albritton testified that Love had been taken from the room while he was at supper, the door having been unlocked from the outside, and the Leader said the size of the mob could not be learned. No report of arrests, indictments or a trial appears in the coverage.

The first reports came from a New Orleans wire story printed on August 24 by the New York Sun under the headline "Negro Boy Lynched" and by the Washington Evening Times as "An Incendiary Lynched." The Alexandria Gazette ran the same text under "Lynched." beside a separate report of a mob killing in Louisiana. These items stated the robbery, arson and confession as fact and gave the lynching itself a single sentence.

The Brookhaven Leader, the county-seat weekly, printed the fullest account on August 29 under "Lynching Near Norfield," drawing on the sheriff and the inquest. It reported the confession as something "it is stated" Love made, called the decoy "a very clever ruse," and faulted Albritton for having "indiscreetly" announced the sheriff's coming, but offered no editorial judgment on the lynching. No Black-press coverage of the killing was found.

The wire story said officers conveying Love to the county jail were overpowered by a mob that hanged him by the roadside. The Leader, a local paper citing the sheriff and inquest testimony, instead said Love was taken from a locked room at the justice's house while no officer was with him. The two also differ on the fire: the wire said the family barely escaped with their lives, while the Leader said they were away at church, and the wire spelled the owner's name "Sassero" rather than "Sasser."

reader.title: Lynching of Irvin Love
bases: A mob took Love, a prisoner accused of burglary and arson, from custody and hanged him (A2, A3, A5).

Love was hanged by a 'mob' after being taken from legal custody (A2, A5); the Leader says three men took part in decoying the sheriff alone, and the killing followed an accusation of robbery and arson (A5).

The New Orleans wire (A2, A3) and the independent local Brookhaven Leader (A5) agree that Irvin Love, accused of robbing and burning the Sasser/Sassero house, was taken by a mob and hanged near Norfield, though they differ on how he was seized.

accounts.label: Wire report (New Orleans)
accounts.gist: Love confessed and returned most of the stolen property; officers conveying him to the county jail were overpowered by a mob, which hanged him to a roadside tree.

accounts.label: Local paper and Sheriff Applewhite (Brookhaven Leader)
accounts.gist: Love was locked in Justice Albritton's back room awaiting the sheriff; friends of the mob decoyed the sheriff with false messages, and Love was taken from the room, the door unlocked from outside, and found hanged next morning.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death at the hands of parties to the jury unknown.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Negro Boy Lynched' and 'An Incendiary Lynched' with the subhead 'A Negro Boy Confesses Crimes and Is Hung by a Mob' stated the crime and confession as fact.
The Leader's 'Lynching Near Norfield' detailed the confession and the ruse on the sheriff, called Albritton's disclosure indiscreet, and reported the coroner's verdict without editorial comment.
